name: Cassava Nkrumah-Volkov
description: A Shelf-born muralist and oral archivist operating out of the collapsed transit tunnels beneath the Kedzie Interchange, Cassava documents the lives of Tier 1 residents through massive accumulative wall paintings that incorporate scavenged chrome, fabric scraps, and bioluminescent fungal paste. Her work is never signed with her real name — instead she leaves a small painted cassava root as a mark, and her identity is an open secret that nobody reports. She broadcasts raw audio walks through her murals on a pirate neural-cast called Wallspeaking, where listeners feel the texture of the concrete under their palms via haptic overlay.
cultural_impact: Wallspeaking has become a de facto memorial archive for Shelf communities that corporate media ignores — several of her murals have been cited in synthetic rights legal briefs as evidence of community identity formation. Her cassava-root tag has been adopted as a solidarity symbol across Tier 1-2 neighborhoods.
story_hooks: A Tier 4 corporate art curator offers Cassava a gallery deal — and the mural she'd have to abandon to accept it depicts a corporate atrocity the corponation wants buried.
One of Cassava's murals begins physically changing overnight, as if something in the Underworld is rewriting it — and the changes are revealing names of people who haven't gone missing yet.
A player needs Cassava's archive to prove a Shelf community existed before a corponation claims the land was uninhabited — but Cassava won't hand over her life's work without trust being earned.
controversy: In 2214, a corponation demolition crew destroyed three of her murals to clear land for a logistics hub; Cassava reappeared the next morning and painted the crew's supervisor's face 40 feet tall above the rubble with the words 'He knew.' The supervisor resigned within a week.
